newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British election result spoils Patten's tennis.
newsitem.headline: British election result spoils Patten's tennis.

text.p: The mastermind of Prime Minister John Major's victory in the 1992 British election, Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten, was playing tennis when he heard of Major's defeat on Friday. "Oh No!" Patten gasped.
But it was not clear if it was the poll results or his tennis game that upset the man tipped as a possible new Tory party leader.
Patten later issued a brief statement congratulating Labour Party leader Tony Blair on his triumph, and voiced hope the new government would maintain British policy on Hong Kong.
Patten was chairman of the Conservative party in 1992 and widely credited with stage-managing Major's election triumph.
Patten, 53, is an avid tennis player and was on his artificial surface court for his daily breakfast-time game when news of Major's crushing defeat by the Labour Party filtered in.

Observed from a slope 100 metres (yards) away in the public gardens which overlook the colonial governor's mansion on Hong Kong Island, Patten could be seen playing doubles, partnered by a brunette against his wife Lavender and a male tennis coach.
Patten's office declined to identify the governor's partners. "They are just regular partners," a spokesman said.
Patten began the game in fine fettle and high spirits, with frequent thumbs-up signals to his partner when she scored a point.
He pumped the air with his fist when he was about to win a game, and raised his hand in a high-five gesture towards his wife at the end.
Patten played well, returning good shots from Lavender's partner and making a number of good returns, but he double-faulted twice on his own serves.
He frequently adjusted his shorts and sweated profusely, wiping his brow often in the tropical heat.
He took several drink breaks at the side of the court, set within the grounds of Government House under tropical trees filled with squawking white and yellow parrots.
Patten took a phone call between rallies, and turned and muttered to his wife, whose mouth fell open in an astonished gasp. This was around the time when the election results were coming in.
He shouted "Oh No!" in anguish several times whenever his game slipped, but it was not clear if this was because the poll results showing Labour galloping toward a landslide victory were on his mind.
Patten has often joked about his tendency to gain weight since arriving in Hong Kong, not helped by the self-confessed gourmand's passion for Chinese food.
"He has taken up tennis to trim his waistline," a friend said.
